Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(\overline{BD}\). Since arc \(BCD\) is a semicircle of radius \(5\), we have

\[
BD=10,\qquad MB=MC=MD=5.
\]

Since arcs \(AB\) and \(AD\) are quarter-circles of radius \(5\), their chords satisfy

\[
AB=AD=5\sqrt2.
\]

Thus \(\triangle ABD\) has side lengths \(5\sqrt2,5\sqrt2,10\), so it is a right isosceles triangle. Hence \(A,B,C,D\) form a square whose diagonals are both \(10\).

The area of this square is

\[
\frac{10\cdot 10}{2}=50.
\]

Now compare the curved region to the square. The semicircular arc \(BCD\) adds two \(90^\circ\) circular segments outside the square, while the two quarter-circle arcs \(AB\) and \(AD\) remove two congruent \(90^\circ\) circular segments inside the square. These added and removed segments have equal areas, so they cancel.

Therefore the area of the curved region equals the area of the square:

\[
50.
\]

The answer is 50.
